Keywords: Gut microbiota, Oral microbiota, Ischemic stroke, Oral-gut axis, Short-chain fatty acids, Tryptophan metabolism Introduction Ischemic stroke (IS) occurs due to temporary or permanent interruption in blood flow to the brain (Qaja and Tadi 2024 ). This condition can result in significant brain injury, leading to lasting neurological deficits, dementia, or even death. Stroke is the second leading cause of death and third in disability worldwide (Saini et al. 2021 ). IS accounts for (85%) while hemorrhagic (15%), approximately 24.9 million cases reported annually, imposing a serious burden on socioeconomic and medical conditions (Benjamin et al. 2018 ). Approximately 90% of stroke cases have been reported to be associated with behavioral factors such as hypertension, diabetes, and atherosclerosis. Microbial dysbiosis also have been shown to play a significant role in the pathogenesis of ischemic stroke through signal transduction, immune regulation, and metabolic function (Benesch et al. 2021 ), altering the body’s response to ischemic events, impacting the overall prognosis of the stroke (Honarpisheh et al. 2022 ). Microbiota-gut-brain axis (MGBA) is a bidirectional communication network between gut microbes and the brain (Khan et al. 2024 ). Gut microbes and their metabolites regulate the transmission of brain neurotransmitters (such as serotonin and catecholamines) through neural, immune, humoral, and endocrine pathways (Sorboni et al. 2022 ). Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) is an immunogenic endotoxin produced by gram-negative bacteria (such as Yersinia pestis , Klebsiella pneumonia , Pseudomonas aeruginosa , Porphyromonas gingivalis , Bifidobacterium species , Chlamydia trachomatis and Francisella tularensis ). LPS can directly cause neuroinflammation or peripheral immune cells to migrate into the brain (Kalyan et al. 2022 ). Intestinal dysbiosis alters immune homeostasis in the small intestine leading to an increase in regulatory T cells and a reduction in IL-17(+) γδT cells. These cells then migrate from the small intestine to the brain, where they cause infarct damage (Benakis et al. 2016 ). IS can lead to impaired intestinal barrier function and increases microbial metabolites, such as trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO), which directly regulate the hyperreactivity of platelets in the body, accelerating the formation of thrombi (Zhu et al. 2016 ). On the other hand, these substances are translocated into the bloodstream, which subsequently accelerates the deterioration of symptoms, leading to poor prognosis for stroke patients (Zhu et al. 2016 ; Swidsinski et al. 2012 ). Recent studies have identified the presence of periodontal pathogens in cerebral aneurysms samples and thrombi from patients experiencing acute ischemic stroke (Patrakka et al. 2019 ; Pyysalo et al. 2016 ). Porphyromonas gingivalis and Streptococcus sanguinis have been detected in these clinical specimens, suggesting a potential link between oral health and cerebrovascular events. This association highlights the role of oral microbial infections in the pathogenesis of ischemic stroke, as these pathogens may contribute to inflammatory processes and thrombus formation (Haraszthy et al. 2000 ). Epidemiological studies further support this link, showing that a higher number of dental caries, periodontal disease, or more tooth loss is associated with a higher risk of IS, while regular dental care may reduce it (Sen et al. 2018 ). The oral and gastrointestinal tracts are intimately connected, forming an “oral-gut axis” that facilitates the translocation of oral microbes to the intestine. Recent studies utilizing high-throughput sequencing technology have demonstrated the biological homology between oral and gut microbiota. The oral microbiome can colonize the intestine, leading to intestinal microbial dysbiosis (Mo et al. 2022 ), indicating the importance of the oral-gut axis in the diagnosis and treatment of diseases (Park et al. 2021 ). Studies have shown that Porphyromonas gingivalis entering the circulation system could be captured and engulfed by neutrophils, leading to their activation (Freiherr Von Seckendorff et al. 2024 ), and the systemic inflammatory burden elevated stroke susceptibility (Palm et al. 2014 ). Oral microbiota not only invade the trigeminal nervous system and blood to promote the production of peptide β-amyloid (Sureda et al. 2020 ), but also directly or indirectly affect the behavior of glial cells through the gut microbiota and its metabolites (Margolis et al. 2021 ). However, the specific patterns of oral and gut microbial co-dysbiosis in IS patients, the extent of oral-to-gut translocation, and the functional metabolic consequences of these changes remain poorly understood. Therefore, this study employed 16 S rRNA full-length sequencing to characterize the oral and gut microbial communities and the overlap and potential translocation of bacteria. Evaluate the alterations in fecal metabolites to elucidate the potential mechanisms linking the oral-gut-microbial axis to ischemic stroke pathogenesis. Materials and methods Study design and specimen collection This is an observational study. This project was approved by the Ethics Committee of the First Hospital of Lanzhou University (LDYYLL2022-513). Clinical trial numbers are not applicable. All methods were performed in accordance with the relevant guidelines and regulations of the institution. Patient recruitment was conducted in the neurology inpatient department between January, 2023 and May, 2024, and all participants were aged between 20 and 76 years. Inclusion criteria (1) Over 18 years of age; (2) Have new ischemic stroke diagnosed by head computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) within 3 days of onset; (3) Have two major ischemic stroke subtypes; large-artery atherosclerosis (LAA) and small-artery occlusion (SAO) according to the Trial of ORG 10,172 in Acute Stroke Treatment (TOAST) classification; (4) Have not received probiotics or antibiotics within one month prior to enrollment. Exclusion criteria (1) Have cardioembolism (CE), stroke of other determined etiology (SOE), and stroke of undetermined etiology (SUE); (2) Have severe heart, liver, or kidney-related diseases; (3) Have diagnosed intestinal or metabolic disorders; (4) Users of proton pump inhibitors, such as omeprazole. A questionnaire was completed for each individual at the time of samples collection to record demographic and other relevant information such as smoking, drinking and clinical history, and oral examination results were recorded. Assess risk by using the national institutes of health stroke scale (NIHSS). Periodontitis is defined as ≥ 4 teeth with ≥ 1 site having probing depth of ≥ 4 mm, clinical attachment loss of ≥ 1 mm, and bleeding on probing. To specifically collect subgingival plaque, a sterile Gracey curette was inserted into the periodontal pocket until resistance was felt at the base of the pocket (approximately 4–6 mm depth) on the lingual side of the mandibular first molars. The curette was then gently scraped against the root surface to dislodge the subgingival plaque (Kim et al. 2023 ). The collected plaque was then placed in a sterile cryopreservation tube and stored in a -80 °C refrigerator for further analysis. 5 g of stool sample was collected from each participant approximately within 48 h after admission using a stool collection container with a tightly screwed lid and sealed with parafilm. Blood parameters and C-reactive protein (CRP) were analyzed using an automatic blood analyzer system (Sysmex XN-20; Kobe, Japan). Biochemical parameters were analyzed using a fully automatic biochemical analyzer (Beckman Coulter AU5800, California, USA). DNA extraction and 16 S rRNA sequencing The full-length (V1-V9) bacterial 16S rRNA gene sequences were amplified using barcoded 27F (5’- AGRGTTYGATYMTGGCTCAG-3’) and 1492R (5’- RGYTA CCTTGTTACGACTT-3’) primers. Both forward and reverse 16 S primers were tailed with sample-specific PacBio barcode sequences to allow for multiplexed sequencing. The amplification of DNA was performed using KOD One PCR Master Mix (TOYOBOLife Science, Osaka, Japan) with the following protocol; initial denaturation step at 95 °C for 2 min, followed by 25 cycles of denaturation at 98 °C for 10 s, annealing at 55 °C for 30 s, and extension at 72 °C for 1.5 min, and a final step at 72 °C for 2 min. Subsequently, the PCR amplicons were purified using VAHTSTM DNA Clean Beads (Vazyme, Nanjing, China) to remove residual primers and nucleotides. The concentration of purified DNA was quantified using the Qubit dsDNA HS Assay Kit and Qubit 3.0 Fluorometer (Invitrogen, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Oregon, USA). SMRTbell libraries were prepared from the amplified DNA by SMRTbell Express Template Prep Kit 2.0 according to the manufacturer’s instructions (Pacific Biosciences, California, USA). LC/MS non-targeted metabolomics analysis Weigh 110 mg of sample tissue, add 1000 µL of extract containing internal standard, vortex mix for 30 s, and ultrasonicate for 10 min (ice water bath). The LC/MS system used for metabolomics analysis consisted of a Waters Acquity I-Class PLUS ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography coupled to a Waters Xevo G2-XS QTOF high-resolution mass spectrometer. The chromatographic column being an Acquity UPLC HSS T3 column (1.8 μm 2.1*100 mm) (Waters, Massachusetts, USA). In mass spectrometry analysis, a data acquisition cycle includes the simultaneous collection of both low and high-collision energy data using a dual-channel setup. The low collision energy is set at 2 V while the high collision energy ranges from 10 to 40 V. The scanning frequency is set at 0.2 s per mass spectrum to accurately capture the desired data distribution. The raw data collected using MassLynx (v4.2) were processed using Progenesis QI software (v2.0), including peak extraction and peak alignment, based on the online METLIN database and Biomark’s self-built library for identification, and at the same time, theoretical fragment identification and mass deviation all are within 100 ppm. Statistical analysis Demographic data were compared between groups using SPSS software (v27.0). Comparisons were conducted using a variety of statistical methods, including two independent-sample t-test, the Chi-Square Test, and Fisher’s exact test. The bioinformatics analysis of this study was performed with the aid of the BMKCloud ( http://www.biocloud.net/ ). The qualified sequences with more than 97% similarity thresholds were allocated to one operational taxonomic unit (OTU) using USEARCH software (v10.0). R software (v3.6.1) was used to draw a Venn diagram and bubble chart. Alpha diversity was assessed to identify the complexity of species diversity of each sample utilizing QIIME2 software (v2023.5). Beta diversity calculations were analyzed by Non-MetricMulti-Dimensional Scaling (NMDS). Wilcoxon test was used to compare bacterial abundance and diversity. Linear discriminant analysis (LDA) was applied to evaluate the differentially abundant taxa. Random forest analysis was performed to compare the microbiome characteristics. After normalizing the original peak area information with the total peak area, the follow-up analysis was performed. Principal component analysis (PCA) was used to judge the repeatability of the samples within the group and the quality control samples. The ropls package (v1.6.2) was used to perform Orthogonal Partial Least Squares Discriminant Analysis (OPLS-DA) modelling, and 200 times permutation tests were performed to verify the reliability of the model. Identified compounds were annotated and mapped to pathways using the KEGG database. Metabolites with the VIP value > 1 as well as Fold Change (FC) > 1 were further applied to a t-test ( P < 0.05) to measure the significance of each metabolite. Enrichment analysis of KEGG pathways was performed using a hypergeometric distribution test. Correlations between microbial taxa and metabolic profiles were assessed using Spearman rank correlation. To account for multiple hypothesis testing, false discovery rate (FDR) control was applied using the Benjamini-Hochberg method. Adjusted Q-values are reported alongside raw P-values for all relevant analyses, including microbial differential abundance, metabolite features, correlation analyses, and KEGG enrichment. Results Characteristics of cohorts Demographic and clinical characteristics of the participants are summarized in Table 1 . Univariate analysis revealed that individuals with ischemic stroke had significantly elevated serum levels of homocysteine (HCY) and C-reactive protein (CRP) compared to healthy controls ( P < 0.05). Additionally, the prevalence of periodontitis and poorer oral hygiene habits was significantly higher in the IS group. Table 1. The P -value is calculated by a Independent Sample t-test, the Chi-Square Test, and Fisher’s exact test To further investigate whether these factors were independently associated with IS after controlling for potential confounders, multivariate logistic regression analysis was performed (Table S1 ). After adjustment, the associations of hyperhomocysteinemia, CRP, and HCY levels with IS were attenuated and no longer reached statistical significance ( P > 0.05). This attenuation suggests that the impact of these traditional risk factors on ischemic stroke risk may not be direct and could potentially be mediated or confounded by other mechanisms, such as the alterations in oral and gut microbiota, which is the focus of this study. Additionally, likely due to the limited sample size of this pilot study, the model yielded wide confidence intervals. Therefore, these results should be interpreted with caution and also require verification in a larger cohort. Composition and diversity of gut and oral microbiota The number of shared OTUs in the intestinal and oral microorganisms of IS patients was 10,763 (Fig. 1 A), which was significantly higher than the number of shared OTUs in the healthy controls, which was only 3,591 (Fig. 1 B). Among the top ten genera, Streptococcus , Neisseria , Ligilactobacillus , Leptotrichia , Blautia , Veillonella , and Capnocytophaga were observed to be shared genera in both the intestine and the oral cavity (Fig. 1 C-D). The content of Streptococcus , Neisseria , Leptotrichia , Veillonella , and Capnocytophaga in the FS group was significantly lower than that in the KS group, while the change in the FC/KC was the opposite. Similarly, the content of Ligilactobacillus and Blautia in the FS group was significantly higher than that in the KS group; conversely, the change in the FC/KC group displayed opposite levels. A total of 27,727 OTUs were identified based on the conventional criterion of 97% similarity in 57 fecal samples. The number of unique OTUs in the FS group was 16,114, which was much higher than that in the FC group (Fig. 1 E). The top 10 genera of the intestinal microbiota include Escherichia , _Shigella , Blautia , Bacteroides , Ligilactobacillus , Streptococcus , Bifidobacterium , Ruminococcus , Faecalibacterium , Subdoligranulum , and Romboutsia (Fig. 1 G). In the 57 oral samples, a total of 8,900 OTUs were shared between the KS group and KC group (Fig. 1 F). Among the top ten species, only the Neisseria was found in the KS group at higher contents than in the KC group (Fig. 1 H). In terms of α diversity, the richness and evenness of intestinal microbial flora between the two groups were statistically significant(Shannon index P < 0.05, ACE index P < 0.05)(Fig. 2 A-B), and the diversity of the FS group was higher than that of the FC group. The similarity of bacterial community structure between FS and FC groups was evaluated by NMDS, which showed a clear separation between the gut microbiome composition of FS and FC groups characterized by Wilcoxon test P < 0.05 (Fig. 2 C). The KS group was significantly higher than the KC group in oral microbial diversity (shannon index, P < 0.05; ACE index, P < 0.05) (Fig. 2 D-E). Similarly, the community structures of the two groups were clearly separated as analyzed with Wilcoxon test P < 0.05 (Fig. 2 F). Identification of biomarkers in patients with ischemic stroke (IS) Linear discriminant analysis (LDA) was used to explore the changes between the oral and intestinal microbiota under different physical states ( P < 0.05, LDA > 4) (Fig. 3 A-B). At the genus level, the oral and intestinal biomarkers of IS patients were similar to those of healthy controls, with eight overlapping bacterial genera respectively, including Capnocytophaga , Neisseria , Fusobacterium , Selenomonas , Streptococcus , Veillonella , Prevotella , and Leptotrichia in the oral cavity and Faecalibacterium , Ruminococcus , Dorea , Romboutsia , Bifidobacterium , Blautia , Escherichia ,_ Shigella , and Subdoligranulum in the gut, which was similar to previous findings (Tan et al. 2021 ; Liao et al. 2022 ). On the other hand, each group has unique enriched bacterial genus in oral cavity and gut. The unique flora enriched in the KS group was Aggregatibacter , and in the FS group was Agathobacter , Eubacterium , Streptococcus , Limosilactobacillus , and Ligilactobacillus (Fig. 3 A). Lachnoanaerobaculum and Campylobacter were unique flora enriched in the KC group, and Bacteroides , Holdemanella and Akkermansia were unique flora enriched in the FC group (Fig. 3 B). Similarly, at the genus level, Subdoligranulum , Streptococcus , and Limosilactobacillus were enriched in the FS group when compared with the FC group (Fig. 3 C). Meanwhile, Bacteroides , a type of bacteria that produces short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), was lacking in the FS group. In the oral microbiota, the biomarkers in the KS group were Neisseria and Massilia (Fig. 3 D). The ANOVA test was used to screen out the significant bacteria with a relative abundance greater than 0.1% (Fig. 3 E), and it was found that the Bacteroides ( P < 0.001, Q < 0.001), Parabacteroides ( P < 0.001, Q = 0.004), Roseburia ( P < 0.001, Q = 0.007) and Holdemanella ( P < 0.001, Q = 0.008) in the FC group was significantly higher than that in the FS group. These are all beneficial intestinal bacteria that generate SCFAs, can improve metabolism, and reduce inflammation (Cui et al. 2022 ; Romaní-Pérez et al. 2021 ; Tamanai-Shacoori et al. 2017 ). The Lachnoanaerobaculum , is also involved in the production of beneficial compounds such as butyrate, acetate, and glucosidase, in the oral specimens of the KC group was significantly higher than that in the FC group (Fig. 3 F) ( P < 0.001, Q = 0.002) (Hedberg et al. 2012 ). Porphyromonas , a periodontal pathogen, was significantly higher in the KS group compared to the KC group ( P = 0.004, Q = 0.049). The correlation between intestinal and oral microbiota The intestinal and oral microbiota of patients with IS interact synergistically, exhibiting a positive correlation (Fig. 4 A). The presence of harmful bacteria may lead to the activation of some opportunistic pathogens, resulting in their own virulence enhancement and changes in the host immune status (Tay et al. 2016 ). There was a positive correlation between periodontal disease-related bacterial genera with the KC group, such as Neisseria and Aggregatibacter , Prevotella and Selenomonas . The core intestinal bacteria genus Lachnoclostridium is negatively correlated with a variety of opportunistic pathogens, such as Capnocytophaga , Fusobacterium , and Campylobacter (Fig. 4 B). These were a normal part of bacterial colonization in the human body. We further used Source Tracker to determine the contribution of oral microbes to the gut in stroke patients, where 61.85% of the gut microbiota came from the oral cavity (Fig. 4 C), and 58.35% of the gut microbiota in healthy controls came from the oral cavity (Fig. 4 D). There was no significant difference between the two groups (Wilcoxon test, P = 0.193) (Fig. 4 E), which again verified the influence of oral microbes on the structure of gut microbiota. Association between microorganisms and clinical factors Spearman correlation analysis was performed to explore the correlations between the microbiome and blood indicators and Periodontitis. The results showed that among the top ten species abundance in intestinal, the bacteria enriched in the FS group were positively correlated with the risk factor. A trend of positive association was observed between Ligilactobacillus and Hyperhomocysteinemia ( P = 0.026, Q = 0.129), Bifidobacterium was positively associated with Hyperhomocysteinemia ( P = 0.011, Q = 0.120), Hyperlipidaemia ( P = 0.029, Q = 0.195) and CRP ( P = 0.010, Q = 0.103). Streptococcus was positively correlated with periodontitis ( P = 0.022, Q = 0.037), and Ruminococcus was positively associated with WBC ( P = 0.021, Q = 0.120). Blautia and Romboutsia were positively associated with folic acid ( P = 0.008, Q = 0.051; P = 0.010, Q = 0.361). By contrast, the beneficial intestinal bacterial were negatively correlated with risk factors, such as Faecalibacterium was negatively correlated with uric acid ( P = 0.039, Q = 0.389), and Bacteroides was negatively correlated with Hyperlipidaemia ( P = 0.049, Q = 0.425) (Fig. 5 A). Among the top ten oral bacteria, Campylobacter was positively correlated with glycated haemoglobin ( P = 0.048, Q = 0.619), folic acid ( P = 0.03, Q = 0.619), and brushing time ( P = 0.02, Q = 0.234) (Fig. 5 B). Therefore, we screened the bacteria enriched in the oral flora of patients with ischemic stroke and analyzed their correlation with risk factors. A relatively small proportion of oral bacteria, such as Bifidobacterium (HCY: P = 0.022, Q = 0.036; Period: P = 0.003, Q = 0.046), Pseudomonas (HCY: P < 0.001, Q = 0.005; Period: P < 0.001, Q = 0.002), Ruminococcus (HCY: P < 0.001, Q = 0.017; Period: P < 0.001, Q = 0.017), Massilia (HCY: P < 0.001, Q = 0.006; Period: P < 0.001, Q = 0.003), Bacillus (HCY: P = 0.002, Q = 0.033; Period: P < 0.001, Q = 0.008), Rhodanobacter (HCY: P = 0.003, Q = 0.046; Period: P < 0.001, Q = 0.007) and Sphingomonas (HCY: P = 0.002, Q = 0.028; Period: P < 0.001, Q = 0.005), have been found to have a direct positively correlation with both homocysteine levels and periodontal disease (Fig. 5 C). Our analysis of a correlation network diagram revealed several key insights: Periodontitis emerged as a central point, showing a notable positive link with alpha diversity indices within the FS group. Specifically, it exhibited the strongest associations with the Chao1 index ( R = 0.397, P = 0.001, Q = 0.03) and the ACE index ( R = 0.317, P = 0.001, Q = 0.03), implying that those with periodontitis tend to possess greater gut microbial species richness. Conversely, hyperhomocysteinemia displayed an inverse relationship with microbial richness, as indicated by the Chao1 index ( R = 0.093, P = 0.007, Q = 0.06) and ACE index ( R = 0.101, P = 0.001, Q = 0.075), suggesting that elevated homocysteine might contribute to reduced gut microbial diversity. Furthermore, frequent toothbrushing (FTB) was significantly and positively related to both Chao1 and ACE indices ( R = 0.183, P = 0.003, Q = 0.045; R = 0.178, P = 0.002, Q = 0.04), reinforcing the connection between oral hygiene practices, microbial richness, and clinical outcomes (Fig. 5 E). In the KS group, the study of the oral microbiota in cerebral infarction patients and their clinical phenotypes revealed that periodontitis had a strong positive correlation with both microbial richness indices (Chao1: R = 0.429, P = 0.001, Q = 0.02; ACE: R = 0.429, P = 0.001, Q = 0.02), thereby indicating a close relationship between periodontitis and significantly elevated oral microbial species richness (Fig. 5 F). Ischemic stroke alters gut microbiota metabolism Unqualified samples were eliminated, and 50 samples were subjected to metabolome qualitative and quantitative analysis (FS = 26, FC = 24). Principal component analysis (PCA) showed that the metabolic phenotypes of the FS group and the FC group were significantly different. The use of orthogonal partial least squares discriminant analysis (OPLS-DA) effectively distinguished between the control and treatment groups (Fig. 6 B), with values of R Y = 0.932 and Q Y = 0.802. This was further confirmed by the permutation test (Fig. 6 C), which demonstrated the stability of the model. 590 metabolites decreased and 550 metabolites increased (Fig. 6 D). Differential metabolic pathways and metabolites To identify the key metabolites in our study, we utilized the KEGG database to annotate the differential metabolites. From the annotated list, we selected the top 20 entries with the most annotations in relevant pathways. Our analysis revealed that the amino acid and lipid metabolism pathways were the most prominent (Fig. 7 A). The top five categories identified in the KEGG metabolic pathway include central carbon metabolism in cancer (Global and overview maps) ( P < 0.001, Q = 0.006), glyoxylate and dicarboxylate metabolism (Carbohydrate metabolism) ( P < 0.001, Q = 0.015), d-Amino acid metabolism (Metabolism of other amino acids) ( P < 0.001, Q = 0.016), protein digestion and absorption (Metabolism of other amino acids) ( P < 0.001, Q = 0.020) and alanine, aspartate and glutamate metabolism (Amino acid metabolism) ( P < 0.001, Q = 0.020) (Fig. 7 B), and radiated 22 differential metabolites. Butyric acid ( P < 0.001, Q < 0.001) and 3-Methylbutanoic acid ( P < 0.001, Q < 0.001) are a short-chain fatty acid metabolite and L-isoleucine ( P < 0.001, Q < 0.001), linatine and L-ornithine ( P = 0.009, Q = 0.040) metabolite derived from of amino acids, which was decreased in the FS group, while the level of L-asparagine ( P < 0.001, Q = 0.005), L-glutamate ( P < 0.001, Q = 0.006), L-aspartic acid ( P = 0.002, Q = 0.010), L-tryptophan ( P = 0.004, Q = 0.019), L-proline ( P = 0.012, Q = 0.049), L-serine ( P = 0.015, Q = 0.057) and L-histidine ( P = 0.021, Q = 0.075) are elevated. In addition, two important metabolites fumarate ( P < 0.001, Q = 0.004), (a fatty acid metabolite), and cadaverine ( P = 0.048, Q = 0.142) (a biogenic amine) were increased in the FS group (Fig. 7 C). Correlation between Microbiome and metabolite Spearman correlation analysis was conducted between differentially abundant metabolites and microbial genera. The beneficial genus Bacteroides showed a positive correlation with butyric acid ( P = 0.042, Q = 0.429). In contrast, bacterial genera enriched in the FS group, including Sphingomonas , Rhodanobacter , Massilia , TM7a and Rhizorhapis exhibited negative correlations with short-chain fatty acids but significant positive correlations with multiple amino acids and cadaverine. Specifically, these genera exhibited significant positive associations with L-Aspartic Acid, L-Tryptophan, L-Histidine, L-Asparagine, and cadaverine, with consistently strong P -values (all P < 0.01) though varying FDR-corrected Q -values (ranging from < 0.001 to 0.213) (Fig. 8 A). For example, Massilia correlated with L-Tryptophan ( P < 0.001, Q = 0.036), L-Aspartic Acid ( P < 0.001, Q = 0.006), L-Histidine ( P < 0.001, Q = 0.033), L-Asparagine ( P < 0.001, Q = 0.036), and cadaverine ( P = 0.002, Q = 0.043). Similar trends were observed for the other genera (Table S2 ). These results suggest a notable link between disrupted amino acid metabolism and gut microbiota composition in the FS group. In a separate analysis, we also explored correlations between oral microbiota and fecal metabolites (Fig. 8 B). There was a significant positive correlation between oral pathogen, Porphyromonas , with the fecal amino acids, L-Aspartic Acid ( P < 0.001, Q < 0.001) and L-Histidine ( P < 0.001, Q < 0.001). Similarly, Bacteroides ( P < 0.001, Q = 0.003) and Pseudomonas ( P < 0.001, Q = 0.002) showed a positive correlation with L-Proline, and Lachnoanaerobaculum showed a correlation with both L-Ornithine ( P = 0.026, Q = 0.212). Sphingomonas were negatively correlated with butyric acid ( P = 0.017, Q = 0.172) and L-Isoleucine ( P = 0.023, Q = 0.198). Although not all correlations remained significant after strict FDR correction, the overarching pattern strongly suggests a link between these microbes and amino acid metabolism dysregulation (Fig. 8 B, Table S2 ). It is important to note that our metabolomic analysis was performed on fecal samples, while the microbiome analysis included both oral and gut sites. Therefore, the correlations between oral microbiota and fecal metabolites (Fig. 8 B) should be interpreted with caution, as they may not reflect direct local interactions but rather point to systemic metabolic alterations or shared influences. Discussion In this study, the association among oral health, gut microbiota, metabolites and ischemic stroke was further examined and verified (Roth et al. 2020 ). While our initial univariate analysis identified elevated HCY and CRP in IS patients, a multivariate model adjusting for multiple covariates did not retain these as independent predictors, a finding limited by sample size and requiring further investigation. The primary and more robust highlight of this study point to the significant associations between IS and distinct alterations in the oral-gut microbiome axis and associated metabolic pathways. The oral microbial signature we observed in IS patients, characterized by an increase in Porphyromonas and Fusobacterium , is highly consistent with the classic “red complex” and associated pathogens that define periodontal dysbiosis (Socransky and Haffajee 2005 ). This suggests that these individuals in our cohort had a concomitant state of periodontal dysbiosis. The mouth serves as a gateway to the gut. Oral pathogens are not only implicated in oral diseases (caries and periodontitis) (Baker et al. 2023 ), but are also associated with an increased risk of systemic diseases (diabetes, cancer, autoimmune diseases and cardiovascular disease) (Graves et al. 2019 ; Yamazaki 2023 ). Even with the protective roles of gastric acid, the intestinal barrier, bile, and pancreatic secretions, the mouth and intestine still share bacterial genera (Segata et al. 2012 ; Kitamoto et al. 2020 ). We observed that the intestinal and oral flora in IS patients showed overlapping bacterial genera, including Streptococcus , Neisseria , Ligilactobacillus , Leptotrichia , Blautia , Veillonella , and Capnocytophaga , which further confirms the concept of the “oral-gut axis” (Lam et al. 2023 ; Kunath et al. 2024 ). The abnormal presence of oral bacteria within the intestine is recognized as a primary factor in disturbing gut homeostasis, potentially inciting an inflammatory response and fostering the transition of the intestinal microenvironment from a healthy to a diseased condition (Segata et al. 2012 ; Kitamoto et al. 2020 ). In the oral cavity, the AgI/II protein family plays a crucial role in the adhesion and virulence of Streptococcus , promoting biofilm formation, platelet aggregation, tissue invasion, and host immune interactions (Abranches et al. 2018 ). In the gut, Streptococcus inhibit inflammatory responses by activating the NF-κB pathway in intestinal epithelial cells and reducing IL-8 production after colonization, thereby maintaining intestinal homeostasis (Kaci et al. 2011 , 2014 ). Ligilactobacillus also has a multifaceted role; it’s frequently employed as a probiotic to boost intestinal metabolic and immune functions (Miri et al. 2024 ). Yet, its proliferation is sometimes detrimental, Ligilactobacillus levels are elevated in a hyperlipidemia model compared to controls (Selmin et al. 2021 ), owing to its significant resistance to unconjugated bile acids, which inhibits bile acid-susceptible microorganisms and leads to its increased abundance (Zhou et al. 2023 ). Thus, it is our conjecture that the heightened level of L. lactis found in the intestines of cerebral infarction patients might signify either a compensatory function or just a quick reaction to external environmental alterations (Chuandong et al. 2024 ). A finding of our study was the overlap and potential translocation of oral pathogens, such as Porphyromonas , Veillonella , and Neisseria , within the gut ecosystem of IS patients, which may be a mechanism linking periodontal disease to cerebral infarction. Porphyromonas colonization of the intestine has been linked to loss of intestinal surface epithelium, destruction of crypt structures, infiltration of inflammatory cells, and enhanced expression of flavin monooxygenase 3 (FMO3), which promotes the conversion of TMA to TMAO, potentially exacerbating intestinal inflammation (Xiao et al. 2021 ). Simultaneously, Porphyromonas induced an increase in branched-chain amino acids levels, activated the AKT/STAT3/NF-κB signaling pathway, and exacerbated microglia-induced neuroinflammation (Shen et al. 2023 ). Furthermore, Porphyromonas has been directly detected in human atherosclerotic plaques, indicating its direct involvement in thrombosis (Haraszthy et al. 2000 ). Clinical studies have shown a positive correlation between the abundance of Veillonella and systemic inflammation levels, stroke severity, and adverse outcomes (He et al. 2024 ). During inflammation in the body, nitrate is a hallmark metabolite of inflammation, and nitrate respiration promotes the growth of Veillonella through the narGHJI operon, thereby increasing its ability to compete and establish in the intestinal environment (Rojas-Tapias et al. 2022 ). Consequently, we propose that the migration of these “shared genera” to the intestine might establish a pro-inflammatory feedback mechanism, thereby elevating stroke risk. This inflammation, in turn, modifies the intestinal milieu, facilitating the colonization of oral microbes. Metabolomic analysis revealed significant alterations in intestinal metabolites after metablic analysis, particularly involving short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) and amino acid metabolism. Concentrations of beneficial SCFAs, such as butyrate and isovaleric acid, were significantly reduced, a finding strongly correlated with decreased abundance of SCFA-producing bacteria including Bacteroides , Roseburia , Lachnospiraceae , and Faecalibacterium (Chen et al. 2019 ; Pryde et al. 2002 ). Butyrate exerts multiple beneficial effects, including enhancing oxidative stress resistance, acting as a histone deacetylase inhibitor to influence gene expression (Bourassa et al. 2016 ), and promoting an anti-inflammatory environment by stimulating IL-10 production while weakening the neutrophil extracellular trap (NETs) and improving intestinal inflammation (Li et al. 2021 ). Tryptophan levels were elevated and positively correlated with multiple bacteria, such as Sphingomonas , Rhodanobacter , Massilia , TM7a , Rhizorhapis and Subdoligranulum . Tryptophan, a microbial-derived metabolite, is produced by various intestinal bacteria including Escherichia coli , Bacillus , Clostridium , and Shigella (Chappell et al. 2016 ). Although tryptophan metabolism can yield antioxidant serotonin via tryptophan hydroxylase (Song et al. 2017 ), its degradation by mitochondrial enzyme monoamine oxidase A (MAO-A) generates reactive oxygen species that disrupt blood-brain barrier integrity and promote apoptosis (Nocito et al. 2007 ). Additionally, tryptophan activates aryl hydrocarbon receptors, exacerbating oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, and vasogenic edema, thereby potentiating brain injury (Sadler et al. 2020 ). In conclusion, our research provides strong evidence for a “mouth-gut axis” whereby ectopic colonization by periodontal pathogens triggers chronic intestinal inflammation, disrupts the integrity of the epithelial barrier, and leads to increased proinflammatory cytokines, which are drivers of atherosclerosis. Metabolomics findings of decreased SCFAs and increased tryptophan further support this mechanism. This understanding suggests that interventions targeting the oral–gut axis such as improved oral hygiene or microbiome modulation, could offer a novel approach to reduce systemic inflammation and lower the risk of stroke. Limitation Despite these findings, our study has several limitations. First, although our sample size ( n = 57) is appropriate for an exploratory multi-omics pilot study, a larger cohort would provide greater statistical power to detect subtler associations and strengthen the generalizability of our findings. Future studies with larger sample sizes are warranted to confirm our results. Second, major confounders such as recent antibiotic use and proton pump inhibitors were controlled through the exclusion criteria. However, other potential confounding factors known to influence the microbiome, such as detailed dietary composition, physical activity, and undiagnosed systemic conditions, were not fully assessed. The influence of these factors cannot be completely ruled out and should be more rigorously controlled in future longitudinal studies. Third, our study is uses of a conventional 97% similarity OTU clustering approach for bioinformatic analysis. While this method is well-established and allows for direct comparison with many previous studies, newer techniques such as Amplicon Sequence Variants (ASVs) offer higher resolution and reduced bioinformatic noise. Future studies could benefit from employing ASV-based pipelines (DADA2 or Deblur) to validate and refine our observations at an even finer taxonomic level. Finally, we did not perform metabolomics profiling on oral samples. Consequently, the functional implications of the oral dysbiosis we observed are inferred from fecal metabolome data or existing literature, rather than being directly measured from the oral environment. Future studies incorporating plaque metabolomics would be invaluable to directly link the oral microbiome with its local metabolic output and further elucidate the oral-gut-metabolite axis in IS. Conclusion This study highlights variations in the gut and oral microbiota of ischemic stroke patients and reveals a complex relationship between these microbial communities and their metabolites. The findings indicate that the FS group exhibited increased microbial diversity, specifically, bacteria that produce tryptophan increased, but lacked beneficial short-chain fatty acid-producing bacteria, which may contribute to dysbiosis. The intestinal and oral flora in IS patients showed overlapping bacterial genera, potentially contributing to microbial dysbiosis. These results underscore the importance of the oral-gut axis in stroke pathology and suggest that targeting microbial dysbiosis may offer new avenues for preventive and therapeutic strategies in ischemic stroke management. PMC Copyright notice PMCID: PMC8888681  PMID: 35250450 Abstract Objective To characterize the intestinal flora of patients with epilepsy and its correlation with epilepsy. Methods Patients with ages > 18 years were consecutively enrolled from the outpatient department, Affiliated Hospital of Guizhou Medical University from January 2018 to December 2019. A total of 71 subjects were recruited, including epilepsy patients ( n = 41) as an observation group and patient family members ( n = 30) as a control group. Fresh stool specimens of all the subjects were collected. The 16S ribosomal RNA sequencing was analyzed to determine changes in intestinal flora composition and its correlation with epilepsy. Subgroup analysis was then conducted. All patients with epilepsy were divided into an urban group ( n = 21) and a rural group ( n = 20) according to the region, and bioinformatics analyses were repeated between subgroups. Results LEfSe analysis showed that Fusobacterium , Megasphaera , Alloprevotella , and Sutterella had relatively increased abundance in the epilepsy group at the genus level. Correlation analysis suggested that Fusobacterium sp. ( r = 0.584, P < 0.01), Fusobacterium mortiferum ( r = 0.560, P < 0.01), Ruminococcus gnavus ( r = 0.541, P < 0.01), and Bacteroides fragilis ( r = 0.506, P < 0.01) were significantly positively correlated with the occurrence of epilepsy ( r ≥ 0.5, P < 0.05). PICRUSt function prediction analysis showed that there were significant differences in 16 pathways between the groups at level 3. Comparing the rural group with the urban group, Proteobacteria increased at the phylum level and Escherichia coli , Fusobacterium varium , Prevotella stercorea , and Prevotellaceae bacterium DJF VR15 increased at the species level in the rural group. Conclusion There were significant differences in the composition and functional pathways of gut flora between epilepsy patients and patient family members. The Fusobacterium may become a potential biomarker for the diagnosis of epilepsy. Keywords: epilepsy, microbiota-gut-brain axis, gut microbiota, 16S rRNA, biomarkers, PICRUSt Introduction Epilepsy is one of the most common and serious nervous system diseases, affecting more than 70 million people worldwide. There are more than 9 million epilepsy patients in China, with approximately 650,000 new epilepsy patients diagnosed each year ( Ngugi et al., 2011 ). Approximately a third of the patients have drug-resistant epilepsy ( Tang et al., 2017 ). The pathogenesis of epilepsy is multifactorial, and the specific mechanisms remain largely unknown. Gut microbes could regulate brain function and behavior through the brain–gut axis ( Johnson and Foster, 2018 ). The brain–gut axis was involved in bidirectional regulation between gastrointestinal functions and the central nervous system. Gut microbiota and their metabolites, such as short chain fatty acids, lipopolysaccharides (LPSs), and amino acids, affected brain function through the brain-gut axis. However, the brain can also affect the gut microbes through the axis by regulating the secretion of intestinal peptides, gastric acid and mucus, intestinal permeability and mucosal immunity through the autonomic nervous system which affect the habitat of intestinal microorganisms, thus affecting the composition of intestinal microbes. The neuroendocrine system can directly affect the intraluminal release of 5-HT, catecholamines and cytokines from enterochromaffin cell, immune cells and neurons on the other hand ( Martin et al., 2018 ). There is a lot of research showed that inflammation plays an important role in the pathophysiology of epilepsy ( Aronica et al., 2017 ). Gut microbes and its secretion can induce the increase of inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 and IL-1 in microglia ( Xu et al., 2021 ), it can also destroy the paracellular barrier via epithelial e-cadherin, which resulting in the increase of blood-brain barrier permeability, and then reducing the response threshold of neurons and improving the excitability of neurons ( Lukiw, 2020 ). Certain intestinal flora could also secrete neurotransmitters such as dopamine, norepinephrine, 5-hydroxytryptamine, acetylcholine, and GABA, which directly or indirectly affected the excitability of the central nervous system ( Jenkins et al., 2016 ; Mittal et al., 2017 ). Therefore, gut microbes may affect the occurrence and progress of epilepsy via the regulation of inflammatory cytokine and neurotransmitter levels. A clinical case-control study showed that the levels of Verrucomicrobia and Actinobacteria in the intestinal tract of epileptic patients were higher than those of normal people at the phylum level ( Gong et al., 2020 ). At the genus level, the levels of Romboutsia , Megamonas , and Bifidobacterium were significantly higher than those of normal humans, while the levels of Sutterella and Klebsiella were significantly lower ( Gong et al., 2020 ). It meant that levels of Bifidobacterium longum , Enterococcus faecium , and Eggerthella lenta could be used as biomarkers for refractory epilepsy. One study reported that at the phylum level, the level of Proteobacteria in the gut of epilepsy patients was significantly increased, compared with the control group, and the levels of Neisseria , Haemophilu s, Delftia , and Lautropia were significantly increased at the genus level ( Şafak et al., 2020 ). Citraro et al. (2021) first characterized the intestinal flora of absence seizure rats (WAG/Rij rats). They found that WAG/Rij rats had a significant difference in intestinal flora, when compared with the normal rats when they were 4-months-old, which mainly involved increased abundances of Clostridiales , Clostridiaceae , and Lachnospiraceae , and decreased abundances of Lactobacillus and Phascolarctobacterium ( Citraro et al., 2021 ). In addition, they found that there already was intestinal villi disruption and inflammatory infiltrates when WAG/Rij rats were 1 month of age, indicating that gut microbiota and epilepsy were interconnected. Medel-Matus et al. (2018) showed that the chronic stress could result to the change of intestinal flora of the rats, and transplantation of intestinal flora of sham-stressed rats into the intestine of chronic stressed rats can partially resist the epileptic effect of chronic stress, and conversely it can increase the susceptibility to epilepsy of sham-stressed rats. Another study showed that fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) could change the composition of intestinal flora. It reported that a child with Crohn’s disease and epilepsy had no seizures in the 20 months of follow-up the FMT treatment ( He et al., 2017 ). In this study, we analyzed the intestinal microbial composition of epilepsy patients and their families based on 16S ribosomal RNA sequencing, and used the random forest prediction model to identify biomarkers for epilepsy diagnosis, to further predict the functional pathways in the gut of epilepsy patients, through which intestinal microbial and epilepsy were linked, so as to provide a new strategy for epilepsy diagnosis and treatment. Materials and Methods Study Participants and Sample Collection Our study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Affiliated Hospital of Guizhou Medical University. The approval number was 146. Patients with epilepsy and their accompanying family members who were examined in the electroencephalogram room or hospitalized in our hospital from November 2018 to June 2020 were divided into the epilepsy and control groups. The enrollment criteria of the epilepsy group were the following: (1) epilepsy patients who met the 2017 ILAE criteria for epilepsy ( Fisher et al., 2017 ) (all types of epilepsy were considered, including focal, general, structural, infectious, immune and hereditary); (2) the patients and their family members lived in the same region; and (3) an age > 18 years. The exclusion criteria were the following: (1) patients who were treated with antibiotics or probiotics (or prebiotics) within 3 months; (2) patients with clear histories of chronic diseases, such as hypertension, diabetes, inflammatory bowel disease, irritable bowel syndrome, and other gastrointestinal diseases; and (3) patients who were complicated with other neurological or psychiatric diseases, such as anxiety, depression, Parkinson’s disease, and Alzheimer’s disease. The enrollment criteria of the control group involved: (1) families of the epilepsy patients as the control group, who lived in the same area with the patients; (2) those who never experienced seizures in their life; and (3) an age older than 18 years. The exclusion criteria were the same as those of the epilepsy group. We have made a survey about type of meal for all the members of families. The control group, coming from the families, has more consistent eating habits with patients. A total of 71 subjects were continuously enrolled in our study, containing the epilepsy group ( n = 41) and the control group ( n = 30). All subjects signed informed consent forms. The participants’ clinical data were recorded, including gender, age, body mass index, ethnicity, residential area (rural or urban), frequency of seizures, course of disease, and use of anti-epileptic drugs. Fresh feces (approximately 200 mg) were sampled using a sampling box (including storage box and cotton swabs, which were all sterile) produced by Omega Bio-Tek (Norcross, GA, United States), and stored at –20°C. Study Design We analyzed and compared the composition of the intestinal flora between the epilepsy and control groups using 16S rRNA analyses, and further investigated the composition and functional pathway differences of the intestinal flora between the two groups using diversity analyses, differential species analyses, random forest analyses, and function predictions. As higher seizure frequencies of epilepsy in rural areas than patients from urban groups (UG) based on our baseline data. In the second part, we conducted a subgroup analysis, and determined the composition of the intestinal flora between the epilepsy patients from rural and urban areas using diversity analysis. Gene Sequencing After sample collection, the intestinal flora DNA was extracted, using a PowerSoil DNA Isolation Kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany), PCR amplification, and sequencing by Shanghai Biotree Biotech (Shanghai, China). V3–V4 regions of the 16S rRNA were amplified by the 515F primer (5′-ACTCCTACGGGAGGCAGCA-3′) and 806R (5′-GGACTACHVGGGTWTCTAAT-3′). PCR products were detected by electrophoresis with 2% agarose gels. A TruSeq DNA PCR-Free Sample Preparation Kit (Illumina, San Diego, CA, United States) was used for construction of a genomic library. The constructed library was quantified by qubit and Q-PCR, and then sequenced by NovaSeq PE250 (Illumina). Bioinformatics Processing For the raw sequences obtained by the Illumina NovaSeq, we performed sequence assembly, filtration, and constructions of chimeras according to the Qiime (version V1.9.1) quality control process, and then we obtained the effective data for subsequent analysis. All effective data of the samples were clustered into operational taxonomic units (OTUs) at 97% identity using Uparse Software (version 7.0.1001). The Mothur method and the SSUrRNA database of SILVA132 were used to perform a species annotation on the OTU sequences. Finally, the sequencing data were rarefied. The species accumulation boxplot and rarefaction curve showed that the sample size was sufficient. The within-diversity of the sample (i.e., α-diversity) was calculated. The inter-sample diversity (i.e., β-diversity) was determined based on the weighted and unweighted Unifrac, and was visualized by principal coordinate analysis (PCoA), which reduced the dimensions of the distance matrix into a two-dimensional graph. The Wilcoxon rank sum test was used for statistical analysis between both groups. Linear discriminant effect size analysis (LEfSe) showed the species with significant differences in abundance among different groups, and identified the intestinal flora with the most biological characteristics, and then calculated the logarithmic linear discriminant analysis (LDA) score (LDA ≥ 3.0 are generally considered to be discriminative). We constructed a random forest model (including the training and test models) based on the relative abundance of intestinal flora of the top 10 at the genus level. MeanDecreaseGin was used to identify important species, followed by cross-validation, constructing a receiver operating characteristic curve, and calculating the area under the curve (AUC) to evaluate the performance of the random forest model. The phylogenetic investigation of communities assessed by reconstruction of unobserved states (PICRUSt) was used for predictions of functions. It inferred gene function profiles based on the gene information on the OTU in the Greengene database, and inferred the gene function profiles of other untested species at the same time. We then constructed a gene function prediction profile of the entire bacterial spectrum, finally “mapped” the sequenced flora data to the database, and performed Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes pathway annotations. Statistical Analysis SPSS statistical software for Windows, version 24.0 (SPSS, Chicago, IL, United States) was used for analysis of the baseline data. Two group means were compared using Student’s t -test and categorical variables were analyzed using the chi-square test. Measurement data are expressed as the mean ± standard deviation (mean ± SD). Spearman’s correlation was used for analysis of the relationship between intestinal flora and epilepsy. A value of P < 0.05 was considered significant. The correlation coefficient |r| between 0.8 and 1.0 meant a very strong correlation, 0.6–0.8 meant a strong correlation, 0.4–0.6 meant a moderate correlation, 0.2–0.4 meant a weak correlation, and 0.0–0.2 meant a very weak or no correlation. Results Demographic Characteristics of the Study Population Between the Epilepsy and Control Groups A total of 41 cases in the epileptic group (EG) and 30 cases in the control group (CG) were enrolled. To decrease the influence of diet on intestinal flora, the control groups were from the families of patients. There was no statistical difference between the EG and CG in average age (31.6 and 34.6 years, respectively), sex (males: 56.1%, and females: 33.3%, respectively), body mass index (BMI) (22.5 and 23.3, respectively), race (Han: 59.5% and other: 60.0%, respectively), place of residence (urban: 51.2 and 46.7%, respectively), and living habits (i.e., smoking, drinking) ( P > 0.05). Among patients with epilepsy, 84.4% involved focal onset. In terms of etiology, 29.3% were structural, 12.2% were infectious, 2.4% were immune, and 56.1% were of unknown origin ( Table 1 ). TABLE 1. Characteristics of Intestinal Flora in Patients With Epilepsy The α-diversity of the EG was slightly higher (the chao1 index of the EG was 345.780, the Shannon index was 0.925, the chao1 index of the CG was 332.142, and the PD_whole_tree index was 0.920) than the CG, but there was no statistical difference ( P > 0.05; the P -values were 0.321 and 0.232, respectively, calculated using the Wilcoxon rank sum test) ( Figure 1A ). PCoA analysis of β-diversity based on the weighted UniFrac distance showed that the composition of intestinal microbes in the EG was different from that in the CG ( Figure 1B ). At the phylum level, Firmicutes was the largest phylum of the EG and CG, but the abundance in the EG was relatively lower than that in the CG (46.6% EG and 50.3% CG), and the Bacteroides was the second largest phylum (44.0% EG and 41.1% CG). The abundance of Fusobacteria showed a significant increase in EG (2.8% EG and 0.8% CG). Some rare microbes had an increased trend in EG, including Verrucomicrobia (0.07% EG and 0.02% CG) and Actinobacteria (0.9% EG and 0.5% CG) ( Figure 1C ). At the genus level, Fusobacterium (2.7% EG and 0.8% CG), Megasphaera (0.54% EG and 0.09% CG), Alloprevotella (1.3% EG and 0.8% CG), Sutterella (1.0% EG and 0.5% CG), and Streptococcus (2.0% EG and 0.04% CG) had higher abundance in the EG ( Figure 1D ). The LEfSe analysis further confirmed the differences of intestinal microbes between EG and CG. In the EG, the abundance of Fusobacteria was significantly increased at the phylum level, the abundance of Fusobacterium, Megasphaera , Alloprevotella , and Sutterella were relatively higher at the genus level, and the abundance of Fusobacterium mortiferum , Prevotella stercorea, Bacteroides dorei , Prevotella sp. Marseille P2931 , Megasphaera elsdenii , Bacteroides fragilis , Ruminococcus gnavus , Ruminococcus torques , Bacteroides eggerthii , and Clostridium sp. AT4 were increased at the species level, while the abundance of Clostridium disporicum , Ruminococcus bicirculans , and Bacteroides coprocola were decreased compared with the CG ( Figures 2A,B ). Correlation Analysis Between Intestinal Microbes and Epilepsy Spearman’s correlation analysis showed that the abundance of Fusobacterium mortiferum , Bacteroides fragilis , Ruminococcus gnavus , and Fusobacterium were positively correlated with epilepsy ( Table 2 ). Characteristics of Intestinal Microbes of Epilepsy Patients in the Urban Group and Rural Group The α-diversity analysis indicated that there was no statistical difference in the intra-sample diversity of the UG, RG, and CG ( P > 0.05), taking observed species index and phylogenetic diversity (PD whole tree) index as examples (calculated by the Kruskal–Wallis Test) ( Figure 5A ). PCoA analysis of β-diversity based on weighted UniFrac distances showed that the composition of intestinal microbes among the three groups was different ( Figure 5B ). At the phylum level, Firmicutes was the largest phylum of the UG, RG, and CG. The abundance of Firmicutes in the RG was lower than that of the UG and CG (49% UG, 44% RG, and 50.3% CG). Bacteroides was the second largest phylum (43.7% UG, 44.0% RG, and 50.3% CG). The abundance of Melainabacteria (0.03% UG, 0.04% RG, and 0.1% CG) and Euryarchaeota (0.001% UG, 0.002% RG, and 0.05% CG) of the UG and RG were decreased, when compared with those of the CG ( Figure 5C ). At the genus level, the abundance of Megamonas (1.0% UG, 0.3% RG, and 0.8% CG) and Subdoligranulum (1.19% YG, 0.06% RG, and 1.12% DG) of the RG were more decreased than those of the UG and CG ( Figure 5D ). Discussion Our results showed abundance difference in the epilepsy group and the control group at the genus level due to our analysis methods (16S ribosomal RNA sequencing). The results did not give absolute amounts of bacteria. We think species and ratios of bacteria were closely with epileptic activity. Therefore, we clarified changes of species and ratios of bacteria in EG and CG. The abundance of Fusobacteria and Verrucomicrobia at the phylum level and Alloprevotella at the genus level were increased in EG when compared with CG. At the species level, Ruminococcus gnavus , Fusobacterium mortiferumis , and Bacteroides fragilis were closely related to epilepsy. Spearman’s correlation analysis further confirmed that Fusobacterium was significantly positively correlated with epilepsy. The random forest model prediction suggested that Fusobacterium played an important role in distinguishing epilepsy and healthy people. This was consistent with the research results of Şafak et al. (2020) who also found significantly increased Fusobacteria in 10.6% of the intestines of epilepsy patients, but not in CG. We think Fusobacteria might be a therapeutic target in the future. The abundance of Verrucomicrobia in patients with epilepsy was increased, which was consistent with a previous study ( Gong et al., 2020 ). Verrucobacterium phylum was positively correlated with serum pro-inflammatory cytokine IFNγ ( Lin et al., 2019 ). It increased the permeability of the blood-brain barrier (BBB) and the small intestinal epithelial barrier by modifying the localization of ZO-1 and claudin-5 ( Rahman et al., 2018 ). As a result, neuroinflammatory substances could easily enter the brain and affect brain function, which was thought to be related to the pathogenesis of epilepsy ( Gao et al., 2017 ). Verrucomicrobia is also associated with the increase of glutamate and glutamine, and decrease of serotonin ( Sun et al., 2016 ), indicating that Verrucomicrobia may be involved in the pathogenesis of epilepsy by affecting neurotransmitter levels. The level of Alloprevotella in patients with epilepsy was increased, which was positively correlated with the occurrence of epilepsy. Alloprevotella can produce SCFAs and have anti-inflammatory effects ( Liu et al., 2018 ; Wei et al., 2018 ), which has been negatively correlated with the level of inflammatory factors such as IL-4 and IL-10 ( Li et al., 2019 ). IL-10 was an anti-inflammatory factor ( Sanjabi et al., 2009 ). Recent studies showed that neuroinflammation can cause high excitability of neurons, leading to seizures ( Sanz and Garcia-Gimeno, 2020 ). Prevotella may be involved in the onset of epilepsy by affecting the levels of cytokines. However, some studies showed that Prevotella produced short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), which have anti-inflammatory effects ( Liu et al., 2018 ; Wei et al., 2018 ), although the mechanism of action needs to be further clarified. In addition, we found the abundance of Ruminococcus gnavus was significantly increased at the species level, which positively correlated with epilepsy. It Ruminococcus gnavus has been confirmed to be closely related to irritable bowel syndrome ( Hall et al., 2017 ), Crohn’s disease ( Nagayama et al., 2020 ), type 2 diabetes ( Wang et al., 2020 ), attention deficit hyperactivity disorder ( Wan et al., 2020 ), and generalized anxiety ( Jiang et al., 2018 ). A previous study showed that Ruminococcus gnavus promoted disease progression by aggravating inflammation and inducing degradation of the intestinal mucosa ( Clark and Mach, 2016 ), which may be one of the mechanisms of epilepsy progression. Fusobacterium mortiferum was also closely related to epilepsy in our study. A study showed Fusobacterium mortiferum was positively correlated with serum levels of 2-deoxy-D-ribose ( Liang et al., 2020 ). The 2-deoxy-D-ribose cooperates with thymidine phosphorylase and vascular endothelial growth factor to inhibit tight junction proteins, leading to the destruction of BBB, which results in inflammatory diseases of central nervous system ( Chapouly et al., 2015 ). In addition, 2-deoxy-D-ribose could also induce neuronal apoptosis through oxidative stress ( Formichi et al., 2009 ), which may be involved in the onset of epilepsy. These studies indicated that Fusobacterium mortiferum and its metabolites may be involved in epilepsy, but no direct evidence has yet been reported. Correlation analysis showed that Bacteroides fragilis was also closely related to epilepsy, which has not been previously reported in epilepsy. Bacteroides fragilis was an anaerobic rod-shaped Gram-negative bacteria that could secrete pro-inflammatory substances, such as LPS and bacteriodes fragilis toxin, which can cause increased permeability of the BBB through E-cadherin of epithelial cells. This made it easier for microbial-derived neurotoxic substances to enter the brain and thus promoted neuronal hyper-excitability and epilepsy ( Vezzani et al., 2016 ; Lukiw, 2020 ). We therefore speculate that Bacteroides fragilis and its metabolites related to epilepsy may induce a neuroinflammatory response by destroying BBB. Our study also showed that the abundance of Bacteroides dorei in patients with epilepsy was increased at the species level. A previous study showed that the colonization of Bacteroides dorei in germ-free mice enhanced the accumulation of TH17 cells ( Nagayama et al., 2020 ), which has been thought to play a central role in the pathogenesis of autoimmune epilepsy ( Han et al., 2020 ). PICRUSt analysis indicated that the upregulation of starch, and sucrose metabolism, and PPAR signaling pathway may be closely related to the onset of epilepsy ( Eor et al., 2021 ). A ketogenic diet can up-regulate the abundance of PPAR in the brains of mice, and then reduce epileptic seizures ( Simeone et al., 2017 ; Eor et al., 2021 ). These results indicated that PPAR pathway could be a target for the treatment of epilepsy. Studies have shown significantly increased abundance of ABC transporter in patients with drug-resistant epilepsy, when compared with patients with drug-sensitive epilepsy ( Peng et al., 2018 ). However, in our study, the abundance of ABC transporter, as well of those of starch and sucrose metabolism, were relatively decreased in patients with epilepsy, and PPAR signaling pathway was significantly increased, which is inconsistent with previous research results. Enriched ABC transporters in the disease group is indeed more meaningful. Contrary results obtained in our study may be related to the insufficient sample size and different populations. We will enlarge the sample size and hope to further determine gut microbiome characteristics of drug-sensitive and drug-resistant epilepsy. Based on the above results, we think the gut microbes may affect the occurrence and progress of epilepsy. There were three possible mechanisms. First, neuroinflammation played an important role in epilepsy ( Yamanaka et al., 2021 ). Proinflammatory cytokines cause morphological changes in human-derived pericyte. Cerebrovascular pericytes undergo redistribution and remodeling contributing to blood-brain barrier (BBB) permeability. Increased BBB permeability was involved in the pathogenesis of epilepsy. Our results showed Fusobacterium, Verrucomicrobia , Alloprevotella , Ruminococcus gnavus , Fusobacterium mortiferum , Bacteroides fragilis , and Bacteroides dorei increased in patients with epilepsy. They may induce proinflammatory cytokines. Second, the increases of glutamate and glutamin were also involved in the process of epilepsy. IL-1 beta influence on glutamate levels was involved in the etiology of both epilepsy and inflammatory bowel disease ( Rindflesch et al., 2018 ). In our study, we also found increased Verrucomicrobia which may be involved in the pathogenesis of epilepsy by affecting neurotransmitter levels. Verrucomicrobia is also associated with increases of glutamate and glutamine, and decrease of serotonin ( Sun et al., 2016 ). Third, hippocampal neuronal apoptosis was closely with progress of epilepsy ( Liu et al., 2019 ). Our results showed Fusobacterium mortiferum increased. It can promote serum levels of 2-deoxy-D-ribose which induced neuronal apoptosis through oxidative stress ( Formichi et al., 2009 ). Because the environment of residence can affect the composition of intestinal flora, with a higher prevalence of epilepsy in rural areas, we determined the differences of intestinal flora between urban vs. rural groups. Our results showed that the abundance of Escherichia coli , Fusobacterium varium , Prevotella stercorea , and Prevotellaceae bacterium DJF VR15 were significantly increased in the RG, and the abundance of Roseburia and Romboutsia were increased in the UG. Certainly, levels of gut microbiota are susceptible to many factors, such as age, gender, diet, geographical location, exercise, drug usage, metabolism, and surgery ( Yang et al., 2021 ). Especially, ketogenic diet can control seizure attack. Akkermansia muciniphila and Parabacteroides played an essential role in the anti-seizure effect of ketogenic diet ( Gómez-Eguílaz et al., 2018 ; Olson et al., 2018 ). Therefore, we also try to apply ketogenic diet to treat patients and explore the relationship of ketogenic diet with gut microbes which we have found in EG in the next experiment. Previous studies showed that 16 representative drugs in the subgroup of the Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical classification system, including anti-seizures medication (ASMs) had no obvious antibacterial effect ( Dahlin and Prast-Nielsen, 2019 ). Consistent with other studies, we found that ASM had no obvious effect on the patient gut microbiome; however, we realize that our sample size was such that this question was underpowered. Limitations Our study had some limitations. First, although we used the 16S rRNA PICRUSt function prediction to analyze the possible mechanism of intestinal flora effects on epilepsy, this was a correlative study, and it did not present direct evidence that increased levels of certain intestinal flora resulted in epilepsy. Studies with larger sample sizes based on metagenomics, proteomics, and metabonomics should therefore be used to further characterize the mechanism of gut microbiota involvement in the pathogenesis of epilepsy. Second, we have not made a subgroup analysis of epileptic patients due to small sample size in EG, such as different etiologies, different types of epilepsies, seriousness of epileptic seizures, effect of ASM, etc. However, we can make further analysis if the sample size is sufficient. Conclusion In summary, there were significant differences in the compositions of intestinal microbes between epilepsy patients and healthy controls. Fusobacterium mortiferum , Bacteroides fragilis , Ruminococcus gnavus , and Fusobacterium sp. may be potential risk factors for epilepsy, and increased levels of Fusobacterium may be a biomarker for the diagnosis of epilepsy. Overall, the characteristic changes of intestinal flora and metabolic pathways in patients with epilepsy suggest that it may be a new target for the treatment of epilepsy. title: Gut dysbiosis is associated with metabolism and systemic inflammation in patients with ischemic stroke
